title: Single Global Lock on Partitionable Data
pattern: A shared multithreaded collection or registry is guarded by a single, monolithic, system-wide mutual exclusion lock (`Mutex` or `RwLock`).
why_bad: Locally, a single global lock is exceptionally simple to write and verify. Globally, it destroys multicore scalability. As more CPU cores or threads are added to the system, thread contention for the single lock spikes, turning the concurrent program into a serialized bottleneck. Threads spend all their time spinning or sleeping, causing latency "tail spikes" when the system is heavily loaded.
detection: A single `Mutex` or `RwLock` wrapping a large collection (e.g., `HashMap`, `BTreeMap`, `Vec`) that is frequently queried or modified by many concurrent threads.
counterexample: A global lock is valid when access frequency is demonstrably low (e.g., once on startup) or when the protected data is extremely tiny and lock hold times are sub-microsecond.
source: Richard L. Sites, *Understanding Software Dynamics*, Chapter 7, "Contention and Locks" (p. 126-127) / 1701.00854v6 (RCU book), Chapter 5.1 (Atomic increment / global counters).
